hook_text: Same exam. Same effort. Different starting lines — and they were drawn by law.
clip_script: Two learners write the same matric exam. One studied in a room with electricity, at a school with a laboratory. The other studied by candlelight after a two-hour taxi trip, at a school with no lab. Same paper. Same effort, maybe. Different starting lines. Now here's the part that makes it economics, not just sadness: those lines weren't natural and weren't accidental. Laws decided who could own land — and took it from most people. Laws decided where families could live, and put them far from work. Laws decided which schools got money. And here's the hard part: repealing those laws stopped the machine — but it didn't undo what the machine built. Land already taken stays taken. A grandmother denied schooling still can't help with homework. A family with no property still has no collateral for a loan. Disadvantage travels down generations. That's why 'the law is equal now' and 'the economy is equal now' are two completely different sentences — and closing the gap between them has a name: redress.
visual_style: Two study scenes side by side — a lit desk and a candle-lit one — then a running track where one lane's start block sits far behind the other, with old statute pages fading into the track markings; a generational chain of houses passing keys and empty hands.
mood: Measured, dignified, factual — no anger, no comfort, just clarity.
pacing: Calm parallel opening, firm middle statement, quiet weight on the closing distinction.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and judge redress with both ledgers open.
